 1                         II.    SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY

 2   Q.   Please describe the purpose of your testimony.

 3   A.   The purpose of this testimony is to respond to the July 7, 2026, Testimony in

 4        Opposition to the Comprehensive Stipulation filed by New Mexico Public

 5        Regulation Commission (“Commission”) Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) witnesses

 6        Daren K. Zigich, Dr. Larry Blank, and Ed Rilkoff, and to support the Commission's

 7        approval of the Comprehensive Stipulation ("Stipulation") filed June 22, 2026, as

 8        a just, reasonable, and in the public interest resolution of this proceeding. To that

 9        end, I address the critical flaw in Dr. Blank's revenue deficiency presentation,

10        Staff's positions on Stipulation Section 1.3 regarding the Cunningham Battery

11        Energy Storage System (“BESS”), issues related to class cost allocation and the

12        system load factor methodology, the demand ratchet implementation, Mr. Rilkoff’s

13        affordability and customer impact arguments, and other matters raised in Staff’s

14        opposition testimony. As explained below, the Stipulation represents a fair and

15        balanced compromise that delivers substantial customer benefits while resolving

16        contested issues without the need for full litigation.

 7           reduction from SPS’s original request of $175,354,544. 2 It incorporates agreed-

12           for the direct assignment of the Cunningham BESS, and includes other rate design

13           and policy resolutions. These outcomes reflect meaningful compromises by all

14           Signatories 3 and provide immediate, tangible benefits to New Mexico customers in

 1        IV.   RESPONSE TO DR. BLANK – CRITICAL FLAW IN REVENUE
 2                         DEFICIENCY PRESENTATION

 3   Q.     Dr. Blank recommends using adjusted jurisdictional allocation factors rather

 4          than the Future Test Year (“FTY”) factors proposed by SPS. What is the basis

 5          for his recommendation?

 6   A.     Dr. Blank’s primary concern with SPS’s proposed Future Test Year jurisdictional

 7          allocation factors is an alleged inconsistency across jurisdictions. He notes that

 8          Texas does not permit the use of a forecasted test year and instead requires a

 9          historical test year with adjustments only for known and measurable changes. Dr.

10          Blank believes that SPS’s use of forecasted allocation factors in New Mexico, while

11          Texas would use historical data, creates a mismatch that could result in over-

12          recovery of revenue requirement across the two jurisdictions. As such, Dr. Blank

13          recommends using adjusted, base period (historical) 12-CP and energy allocation

14          ratios for separating costs between Texas, New Mexico, and the Federal Energy

15          Regulatory Commission (“FERC”).

 1   Q.   What specific adjustments does Dr. Blank propose to the base period loads?

 2   A.   Dr. Blank starts with SPS’s base period 12-CP data and makes three adjustments to

 3        the New Mexico allocation:

 4        •   He removes the effect of forecasted load growth in New Mexico (approximately
 5            524 megawatts (“MW”) for production 12-CP).

 6        •   He removes 100 MW of wholesale production contract demand that SPS is
 7            losing.

 8        •   He reduces New Mexico’s 12-CP by an additional 24 MW to reflect the
 9            accredited capacity of the Cunningham BESS, which SPS proposes to directly
10            assign to New Mexico.

11               These adjustments significantly lower New Mexico’s share of system

12        production and transmission costs relative to SPS’s FTY proposal.

13   Q.   What revenue deficiency does Dr. Blank state results from his

14        recommendations?

15   A.   Dr. Blank states that his adjustments result in a revenue deficiency of $47.7 million

16        — a substantial reduction from SPS’s originally proposed $175.4 million increase.

17        He attributes most of this reduction to his recommended change in jurisdictional

18        allocation methodology.

 1   Q.   Does Dr. Blank’s calculation provide a consistent, apples-to-apples

 2        comparison of the revenue deficiency?

 3   A.   No. His calculation of the resulting revenue deficiency is internally inconsistent.

 4        He applies base period (historical) jurisdictional allocators (which assign lower

 5        costs to New Mexico) but continues to use the higher Future Test Year present

 6        revenues and billing determinants that SPS filed.

 7               In other words, he lowers the allocated revenue requirement using historical

 8        loads but measures the deficiency against higher forecasted sales and revenues.

 9        This mismatch between the cost side (base period) and the revenue side (FTY)

10        produces an artificially low deficiency figure in violation of the matching principle.

11               Simply put, Dr. Blank is assuming load growth will not happen for purposes

12        of allocating costs between SPS’s Texas and New Mexico jurisdictions, but then

13        assumes it will happen for purposes of calculating sales volumes for SPS’s present

14        revenue calculation.

15   Q.   Why is the $47.7 million revenue deficiency figure presented by Dr. Blank

16        misleading?

17   A.   Dr. Blank’s revenue deficiency is misleading because it relies on a mismatch of the

18        period (historical vs. future) sales/load figures used to calculate SPS’s present

 2   As noted above, he assumes SPS’s forecasted sales will occur for the present

 3   calculation but will not occur for the revenue requirement cost allocation. As shown

 4   below, using base period (historical) matching sales/load figure—consistent with

 5   the matching principle—in both the present revenue calculation and revenue

 6   requirement cost allocation, Dr. Blank’s revenue deficiency would be $173.1

 7   million, nearly identical to SPS’s filed case. While it is inappropriate in an FTY to

 8   simply ignore load growth in the forecast, it violates the matching principle to

 9   ignore it for only one half of the equation.

10          As shown in Attachment AGT-STIP-R1, which replicates Schedule P-5, tab

11   (b) of SPS’s filing, the difference in retail revenues at present rates between FTY

12   forecasted volumes and base period volumes is approximately $125.4 million.

13   Adding this amount to Dr. Blank’s stated deficiency produces a revenue deficiency

14   of roughly $173.1 million on a consistent base period basis — very close to SPS’s

15   original $175.4 million request. The following Table AGT-STIP-R1 illustrates the

 4   the superior ratemaking construct. The FTY framework, expressly authorized under

 1        V.   RESPONSE TO STAFF ON STIPULATION CONDITION 1.3 –
 2                      CUNNINGHAM BESS TREATMENT

 3   Q.    Mr. Zigich opposes the agreed-upon valuation methodology for the accredited

4          capacity (“ACAP”) benefits of the Cunningham BESS under Stipulation

5          Section 1.3, arguing it undervalues broader energy storage benefits and

 6         questions the further division by (1 + seasonal PRM). How do you respond?

 7   A.    The Stipulation’s treatment of the Cunningham BESS in Section 1.3 properly

 8         implements the direct assignment of all costs and capacity benefits to New Mexico

 9         retail customers while incorporating the necessary and appropriate adjustment for

10         Southwest Power Pool Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”) that is consistent with

11         the cost causation principles underlying the 12-CP allocator and SPS’s class cost

12         of service study methodology. The accredited capacity of the BESS is

13         approximately 24 MW. However, not all of this capacity serves contemporaneous

14         load in the same manner as other rate-base resources. A portion of the accreditation

15         satisfies Southwest Power Pool’s resource adequacy reserve requirements (seasonal

16         PRMs of 16% summer and 36% winter). The 12-CP production jurisdictional

17         allocator measures each jurisdiction’s relative responsibility for contributing to

18         system peak load. Because the PRM portion represents a reliability buffer above



                                               11
                               Case No. 25-00079-UT
                          Rebuttal Testimony in Support of
                            Comprehensive Stipulation
                                         of
                             Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   peak load - not load-serving capacity - it is appropriately reflected in the valuation

 2   methodology by dividing the seasonal ACAP by one plus the applicable seasonal

 3   PRM, as set forth in Stipulation Sections 1.3(a) and (b). Including the full ACAP

 4   without this adjustment would double-count the benefit and overstate the extent to

 5   which New Mexico’s load relies on shared system capacity resources.

 6          This PRM-adjusted valuation methodology does not “undervalue” the

 7   BESS. It ensures the offset to the 12-CP allocator (as implemented in Stipulation

 8   Section 1.17) accurately reflects the incremental impact of the resource on New

 9   Mexico’s measured peak load responsibility - the precise purpose of the allocator.

10   The Stipulation gives New Mexico 100% of the properly measured capacity benefit

11   through the direct assignment and jurisdictional allocator adjustment, satisfying the

12   condition articulated by Mr. Zigich.

13          Mr. Zigich raises a broader point regarding the energy, market, arbitrage,

14   and ancillary service benefits of the Cunningham BESS. SPS agrees that these

15   operational benefits have real value. However, these benefits are distinct from the

16   capacity benefits used for purposes of the 12-CP jurisdictional allocator. The 12-

17   CP methodology is fundamentally a peak demand and capacity allocation tool. It

18   measures each jurisdiction’s contribution to system coincident peak loads and is

                                            12
                                Case No. 25-00079-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony in Support of
                             Comprehensive Stipulation
                                          of
                              Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   not designed to capture or allocate energy, market, or ancillary service revenues.

 2   The energy, market, arbitrage, and ancillary service benefits of the Cunningham

 3   BESS will be directly assigned to New Mexico customers through the Fuel and

 4   Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause (“FPPCAC”). All associated market

 5   revenues and costs of the unit will flow through the FPPCAC, ensuring that New

 6   Mexico customers receive the full benefit of the BESS’s operational performance.

 7   In this manner, the proposed treatment recognizes the full value of the resource

 8   through the appropriate and established ratemaking mechanisms for each type of

 9   benefit. Mr. Zigich appears to advocate for a holistic valuation of the BESS within

10   the 12-CP allocator itself. Because the 12-CP allocator is fundamentally a capacity-

11   based methodology, it is not necessary nor appropriate to embed energy or market

12   benefits into that allocator.

13           Section 1.3 also commits SPS to initiate a stakeholder process prior to the

14   next base rate case to evaluate the treatment of directly assigned resources and

15   divergent state resource portfolios for future proceedings, preserving flexibility for

16   refinement.

 1   Q.   Dr. Blank criticizes the PRM adjustment in the Stipulation as flawed and

 2        argues that the full accredited capacity should be used to reduce New Mexico’s

 3        12-CP values because resource adequacy requirements are met by rate base

 4        items and the full amount offsets total load including PRM. How do you

 5        respond?

 6   A.   Dr. Blank’s position misreads the purpose of the 12-CP allocator. The allocator is

 7        designed to apportion generation capacity costs in rate base based on each

 8        jurisdiction’s contribution to system peak load. It is not a mechanism to allocate all

 9        resource adequacy obligations or capacity beyond what serves load at the peak. The

10        PRM exists above and beyond peak load as a reliability buffer. Treating the full

11        ACAP - including the reserve component - as a direct reduction to peak load

12        responsibility would be inconsistent with the allocator's load-based design and

13        would effectively allow the same megawatts to both satisfy reserve requirements

14        and reduce peak load responsibility, overstating New Mexico’s benefit. The

15        Stipulation’s PRM-adjusted valuation and corresponding 12-CP adjustment

16        correctly limits the offset to the portion of accredited capacity that directly offsets

17        load. This maintains the integrity of the cost allocation methodology while still

18        providing New Mexico the full benefit of the load-serving capacity from the BESS.

 1        VI.   RESPONSE TO DEMAND RATCHET IMPLEMENTATION

 2   Q.    Dr. Blank does not oppose the demand ratchet modifications but recommends

 3         an 11-month phase-in before the new ratchets take effect. What is SPS’s

 4         position?

 5   A.    SPS supports prompt implementation of the demand ratchet modifications agreed

 6         to in the Stipulation (Section 1.13), under which the LGS-T ratchet demand

 7         increases from the current 60% to 70%. The current ratchet design permits certain

 8         customers within the Primary General and LGS-T classes to avoid paying their

 9         appropriate share of demand-related production and transmission costs, creating an

10         intraclass subsidy borne by other customers in those classes. Implementing the

11         agreed ratchet promptly corrects this misalignment and produces lower rates overall

12         for the classes as a whole once the subsidy is eliminated. Delaying implementation

13         unnecessarily prolongs the subsidy and delays the rate reductions that the cost-of-

14         service study demonstrates are appropriate for the majority of customers in these

15         classes. Customers in the Primary General and LGS-T classes are generally

16         sophisticated industrial and large commercial entities capable of understanding and

17         managing their peak demand in response to price signals. There is no record

18         evidence demonstrating a need for an extended transition period for these

 1 VII.   RESPONSE REGARDING CLASS COST ALLOCATION AND SYSTEM
 2                     LOAD FACTOR METHODOLOGY

 3   Q.   How do you respond to Staff’s assertion that Condition 1.11 conflicts with the

 4        Stipulation approved in Case No. 25-00085-UT?

 5   A.   Staff witness Daren K. Zigich asserts that Condition 1.11 of the Comprehensive

 6        Stipulation in this case (which adopts a 1-CP system load factor for purposes of the

 7        AED-4CP methodology) is “in direct contrast or conflict” with Condition 1.3(C) of

 8        the Unanimous Comprehensive Stipulation approved in Case No. 25-00085-UT. I

 9        respectfully disagree. There is no conflict.

10        Condition 1.3(C) of the Stipulation in Case No. 25-00085-UT states:

11               “SPS shall convene a working group with stakeholders and Staff to evaluate
12               and analyze alternatives to SPS’s current retail customer class cost
13               allocation for both demand (capacity) and energy costs. The results of this
14               analysis will be presented in SPS’s next rate case.”

15        Two fundamental points resolve the claimed conflict:

16               First, the stakeholder working group contemplated by Condition 1.3(C) has

17        not yet been convened, and the evaluation process has not yet occurred. The prior

18        Stipulation does not freeze SPS’s cost-allocation methodology in place pending that

19        future process. It simply commits SPS to a collaborative review whose results will

20        be presented in a future rate case. Nothing in Condition 1.3(C) prohibits the parties


                                               18
                               Case No. 25-00079-UT
                          Rebuttal Testimony in Support of
                            Comprehensive Stipulation
                                         of
                             Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   from agreeing, in the interim, to a specific refinement of the existing methodology

 2   (here, the use of a 1-CP system load factor within the AED-4CP framework) as part

 3   of a comprehensive settlement of the present rate case.

 4          Second, Condition 1.11 of the Stipulation in this case does not “negate” or

 5   undermine the future working group process. On the contrary, the current

 6   Stipulation expressly preserves the ability of the parties and the Commission to

 7   revisit cost-allocation methodologies. The adoption of the 1-CP system load factor

 8   is a discrete, negotiated change that is widely used in the industry and that the

 9   Signatories agreed is reasonable for purposes of this case. It does not preclude the

10   broader evaluation of alternatives that Condition 1.3(C) requires SPS to undertake

11   and present in its next rate case. The two provisions address different things: one is

12   a commitment to future collaborative study; the other is a present-case settlement

13   of a specific methodological detail.

14          In short, Condition 1.11 is fully consistent with—and does not impair—the

15   working group commitment made in Case No. 25-00085-UT. The stakeholder

16   process remains available for a more comprehensive review of class cost allocation,

17   and nothing in the present Stipulation limits or predetermines the recommendations

18   that may emerge from that process. Staff’s claim of conflict is not accurate, and it

 1        provides no basis for rejecting Condition 1.11 or the Stipulation as a whole.

 2   Q.   The Stipulation adopts the use of a single peak demand (“1-CP”) system load

 3        factor in the Average and Excess 4-Coincident Peak (“AED-4CP”) demand

 4        allocation methodology (Section 1.11). How do you respond to Zigich’s

 5        testimony that “This generally has the effect of favoring high-capacity factor

 6        loads to the detriment of residential and small commercial customers with

 7        more variable load factors. Further, the single coincident peak has even less

 8        relevance to the SPP’s new seasonal capacity accreditation and Planning

 9        Reserve Margin values that significantly impact resource needs and thus cost

10        of the system.”?

11   A.   The Stipulation adopts the 1-CP system load factor for the AED-4CP methodology

12        as part of the overall negotiated resolution. The use of a 1-CP system load factor

13        within the AED-4CP demand allocation methodology is a widely accepted and

14        commonly employed approach in cost-of-service studies. By calculating the system

15        load factor based on the single highest monthly peak rather than a multi-month

16        average, the 1-CP method provides a more direct and focused measure of the

17        relationship between a customer class’s average demand and the system’s peak

18        condition. While the choice of system load factor can affect the weighting between

                                              20
                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                               Rebuttal Testimony in Support of
                                 Comprehensive Stipulation
                                              of
                                  Alexander G. Trowbridge

 1   average and excess demand components and thus shift production and transmission

 2   costs among customer classes (generally increasing allocations to lower load factor

 3   classes such as residential relative to higher load factor classes), the stipulated

 4   revenue allocation and gradualism adjustments in Exhibit A to the Stipulation

 5   substantially moderate the resulting bill impacts. The gradualism and banding

 6   approach agreed upon by the Signatories more than mitigates any perceived

 7   increase or shift that might otherwise have occurred from the load factor

 8   methodology alone. For example, based on the stipulated target revenue

 9   requirement of $90 million, the use of a 1-CP system load factor in the AED-4CP

10   demand allocation results in an increase to the Residential General class of $2.3

11   million 4. However, gradualism support for the Residential General class reduces

12   what would otherwise be allocated to the class by $28.5 million 5, far outweighing

13   the perceived increase from the change to 1-CP.

14              The revenue allocation in Stipulation Exhibit A is the product of

15   compromise among the parties and is not strictly dictated by any single

16   methodological choice in the Class Cost of Service Study (“CCOSS”). It balances
